variants.title: Run the reasoning service
variants.context: A reasoning service runs the same five stages for every request: state the claim contract, gate the evidence, execute the engine, verify the mode-specific invariant, then return a supported claim or an explicit abstention.
variants.prompt: A product asks whether an account qualifies for a transfer permission. Put the service stages in order.

items.text: Reasoning engine: deduce, estimate, or adapt within the selected contract.
Evidence gate: admit only facts, assumptions, or support examples compatible with that claim.
Bounded answer: return the supported claim or an explicit abstention.
Verification: test the trace, the uncertainty, and the invariant for that mode.
Request contract: fix the exact conclusion the system may return and its decision boundary.

variants.hint: Which stage stops a fluent interface from quietly changing the question?
variants.explanation: The contract fixes the claim before any engine runs, and the evidence gate rejects incompatible inputs before expensive execution.

variants.title: Run the reasoning service
variants.context: A reasoning service runs the same five stages for every request: state the claim contract, gate the evidence, execute the engine, verify the mode-specific invariant, then return a supported claim or an explicit abstention.
variants.prompt: A request asks for the effect of extending a grace period, but the caller supplies only observational retention counts with no treatment assignment. Put the stages in order for the run that ends in abstention.

items.text: Evidence gate: find that the supplied data cannot identify the estimand and stop the run.
Verification: confirm that no documented adjustment set or assumption graph exists.
Bounded answer: abstain and name the evidence the caller would need to supply.
Request contract: record that the claim is an intervention estimate, not an association.

variants.hint: What is the honest output when the evidence cannot support the requested claim?
variants.explanation: Claim-evidence fit means the system returns only what its representation and evidence support, and abstains otherwise.

variants.title: Run the reasoning service
variants.context: A reasoning service runs the same five stages for every request: state the claim contract, gate the evidence, execute the engine, verify the mode-specific invariant, then return a supported claim or an explicit abstention.
variants.prompt: A hybrid request needs a learned ranker to shortlist evidence and a rule engine to decide admissibility. Put the stages in order for that run.

items.text: Verification: check that each subclaim still carries the trace of the engine that produced it.
Reasoning engine: run each subclaim on its own engine and keep the results separate.
Request contract: split the request into a ranking subclaim and an admissibility subclaim.
Evidence gate: admit reviewed support examples for the ranker and authoritative facts for the rules.
Bounded answer: return the decision with per-subclaim evidence rather than one blended score.

variants.hint: What does a single combined confidence number destroy?
variants.explanation: Composition is safe only when each subclaim keeps its own engine, version, evidence, and uncertainty.

variants.title: Derive a symbolic conclusion
variants.context: A symbolic engine normalizes source records into typed predicates, applies versioned rules with explicit precedence, records the proof trace, and stops at a boundary by answering, requesting a missing fact, or flagging a contradiction.
variants.prompt: A rule engine must decide whether account 42 may transfer funds. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Apply versioned rules: match premises and derive only what the active policy set permits.
Normalize facts: map the source records into typed predicates with provenance and effective dates.
Stop at a boundary: return the conclusion, request a missing fact, or flag a contradiction.
Build the proof trace: record the facts and rule versions supporting each derived conclusion.

variants.hint: The trace is part of the answer, not an afterthought.
variants.explanation: Explicit rules are only as good as their governance, so provenance, versions, and the proof trace travel with the conclusion.

variants.title: Derive a symbolic conclusion
variants.context: A symbolic engine normalizes source records into typed predicates, applies versioned rules with explicit precedence, records the proof trace, and stops at a boundary by answering, requesting a missing fact, or flagging a contradiction.
variants.prompt: A general rule grants access to verified accounts while a more specific rule denies access to accounts under review. Put the steps in order for that query.

items.text: Apply versioned rules: resolve precedence so the specific rule overrides the general one.
Normalize facts: record both the verification fact and the review fact with their validity windows.
Stop at a boundary: return the denial with its trace rather than the first matching answer.
Build the proof trace: name the rule that won, the rule it overrode, and the facts behind each.

variants.hint: Source order is not a precedence policy.
variants.explanation: Precedence between specific and general rules must be defined explicitly, and the trace has to show which rule was overridden.

variants.title: Derive a symbolic conclusion
variants.context: A symbolic engine normalizes source records into typed predicates, applies versioned rules with explicit precedence, records the proof trace, and stops at a boundary by answering, requesting a missing fact, or flagging a contradiction.
variants.prompt: Two ingested records assert contradictory residency facts for the same customer, and a malformed rule cycles. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Stop at a boundary: flag the case for review instead of answering from one arbitrary fact.
Apply versioned rules: hit the inference depth cap that bounds work on the cyclic rule.
Normalize facts: load both residency assertions with their sources and effective dates.
Build the proof trace: record the contradiction and the partial derivation that reached it.

variants.hint: What must a bounded engine do before a malformed rule can run forever?
variants.explanation: Contradictions and cycles are reportable outcomes, and depth caps keep malformed rules from creating unbounded execution.

variants.title: Build a causal estimate
variants.context: A causal result is an assumption-backed estimate. Define the estimand, draw the assumption graph, choose a design and adjustment set that identify it, then challenge the answer with sensitivity and negative-control tests.
variants.prompt: A team wants to know whether a longer grace period improves retention. Put the study steps in order.

items.text: Draw assumptions: encode plausible common causes, mechanisms, selection, and measurement timing.
Define the estimand: state the population, treatment contrast, outcome, and time horizon.
Identify and estimate: pick a design and adjustment set that identify the estimand, then estimate with uncertainty.
Challenge the answer: test alternate graphs, overlap, negative controls, and unobserved confounding.

variants.hint: The graph comes from domain knowledge, not from whatever columns exist.
variants.explanation: Identification depends on the estimand and the graph, so the question and its assumptions are settled before any estimator runs.

variants.title: Build a causal estimate
variants.context: A causal result is an assumption-backed estimate. Define the estimand, draw the assumption graph, choose a design and adjustment set that identify it, then challenge the answer with sensitivity and negative-control tests.
variants.prompt: A model that forecasts retention accurately is offered as proof that the policy works. Put the steps in order for the study that would actually settle it.

items.text: Identify and estimate: adjust for the eligible backdoor path and report the effect with uncertainty.
Define the estimand: separate the total effect of the policy from prediction of the outcome.
Challenge the answer: run a placebo outcome and check sensitivity to unobserved confounding.
Draw assumptions: name account maturity as a common cause of both exposure and retention.

variants.hint: Ask what question a forecast answers and what question an intervention asks.
variants.explanation: Predictive accuracy does not validate a causal claim, because a model can forecast an outcome well and still misestimate an intervention.

variants.title: Build a causal estimate
variants.context: A causal result is an assumption-backed estimate. Define the estimand, draw the assumption graph, choose a design and adjustment set that identify it, then challenge the answer with sensitivity and negative-control tests.
variants.prompt: A randomized rollout is available, but a third of assigned users never received the new policy. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Draw assumptions: encode noncompliance, attrition, and interference between assigned users.
Identify and estimate: use the design that fits the chosen estimand and report uncertainty.
Define the estimand: state whether the target is the effect of assignment or of actual exposure.
Challenge the answer: check attrition balance and whether interference broke the assignment logic.

variants.hint: Randomization simplifies identification, but it does not remove every threat.
variants.explanation: Experiments break the link from pre-treatment causes to assignment, yet noncompliance, attrition, interference, and measurement still need attention.

variants.title: Name the role in the graph
variants.context: A causal graph names roles, not just variables. Treatment is what you can intervene on, outcome is what you measure, a confounder is a common cause of both, a mediator sits on the mechanism, and a collider is a shared consequence.
variants.prompt: A team drafts a causal graph before choosing an estimator. Match each role to what it means.

pairs.label: Treatment
pairs.detail: The variable the team may actually intervene on.

pairs.label: Outcome
pairs.detail: The metric whose response to the intervention is being estimated.

pairs.label: Confounder
pairs.detail: A common cause of both the treatment and the outcome.

pairs.label: Mediator
pairs.detail: A variable that sits on the mechanism running from treatment to outcome.

pairs.label: Collider
pairs.detail: A shared consequence of two variables, which biases results when conditioned on.

variants.hint: Sort by where the arrows point, not by how useful the variable is for prediction.
variants.explanation: Roles are defined by position in the graph, and the adjustment decision follows from the role rather than from data availability.

variants.title: Name the role in the graph
variants.context: A causal graph names roles, not just variables. Treatment is what you can intervene on, outcome is what you measure, a confounder is a common cause of both, a mediator sits on the mechanism, and a collider is a shared consequence.
variants.prompt: Longer grace periods are followed by higher retention. Match each variable in that study to its role.

pairs.label: The length of the grace period the team can set
pairs.detail: Treatment, because it is the input the team can intervene on.

pairs.label: Retention measured ninety days after exposure
pairs.detail: Outcome, because it is the metric whose response is being estimated.

pairs.label: Account maturity, which raises both exposure and retention
pairs.detail: Confounder, because it is a common cause of treatment and outcome.

pairs.label: Fewer failed payments, caused by the longer grace period
pairs.detail: Mediator, because it lies on the mechanism from treatment to outcome.

pairs.label: Support ticket volume, driven by both the policy and churn risk
pairs.detail: Collider, because it is a shared consequence of the two variables.

variants.hint: One of these variables opens a biasing path only if you condition on it.
variants.explanation: Naming account maturity as a confounder is what makes the association-to-effect gap visible before anyone fits a model.

variants.title: Name the role in the graph
variants.context: A causal graph names roles, not just variables. Treatment is what you can intervene on, outcome is what you measure, a confounder is a common cause of both, a mediator sits on the mechanism, and a collider is a shared consequence.
variants.prompt: The estimand is the total effect of the policy. Match each variable to the adjustment decision it deserves.

pairs.label: A confounder on an open backdoor path
pairs.detail: Include it in the adjustment set so the backdoor path is blocked.

pairs.label: A mediator on the treatment mechanism
pairs.detail: Leave it out, since conditioning on it removes part of the total effect.

pairs.label: A collider downstream of treatment and outcome
pairs.detail: Leave it out, since conditioning on it opens a biasing path.

pairs.label: The treatment variable itself
pairs.detail: Never adjust for it, since it defines the contrast being estimated.

variants.hint: More features is not the same as a better adjustment set.
variants.explanation: For a total effect you block eligible backdoor paths without conditioning away the mechanism, so a smaller grounded model can beat a larger one.

variants.title: Guard the adaptation boundary
variants.context: Meta-learning trains across a distribution of tasks. An inner loop adapts using support examples and an outer loop updates reusable parameters against separate query examples, so few-shot scores are evidence about one task family.
variants.prompt: Meta-test tasks were drawn from the same pool that shaped the reusable initialization, and the team reports 91 percent five-shot accuracy. What is the first fix?
options: Split by task so meta-test tasks never contributed to the reusable initialization.
Raise the support size until the reported few-shot score stops improving with more shots.
Add a regularizer to the inner loop so adaptation cannot overfit a single task.
optionFeedback: Correct: task-level splitting is what makes a meta-test score evidence about unseen tasks.
A larger support set changes the operating point but leaves the contaminated split intact.
Regularizing adaptation is reasonable tuning, but it does not remove the leaked tasks from meta-training.
variants.hint: Ask which tasks the reusable parameters have already seen.
variants.explanation: Meta-evaluation splits by task, not by example, so the initialization is never shaped by the tasks used to judge adaptation.

variants.title: Guard the adaptation boundary
variants.context: Meta-learning trains across a distribution of tasks. An inner loop adapts using support examples and an outer loop updates reusable parameters against separate query examples, so few-shot scores are evidence about one task family.
variants.prompt: A report contains one number: five-shot accuracy on the meta-test tasks, with no other run. Which addition makes the result interpretable?
options: Repeat the same five-shot measurement over many more tasks from the same pool.
Publish the inner-loop step count and learning rate so the adaptation can be reproduced.
Report accuracy across support sizes beside fine-tuning and no-adaptation baselines.
optionFeedback: More tasks tighten the error bar on a number that still has nothing to be compared against.
Reproducibility details are useful, but they do not tell you whether adaptation helped at all.
Correct: a shot-count curve plus ordinary fine-tuning and no-adaptation baselines show whether meta-learning earned its cost.
variants.hint: One number at one convenient shot count answers which question?
variants.explanation: Few-shot claims need baselines and a support-size curve, since a single convenient shot count can hide that adaptation adds nothing.

variants.title: Guard the adaptation boundary
variants.context: Meta-learning trains across a distribution of tasks. An inner loop adapts using support examples and an outer loop updates reusable parameters against separate query examples, so few-shot scores are evidence about one task family.
variants.prompt: In production the incoming tasks drift into a family the meta-training distribution never covered, and adapted accuracy falls below the no-adaptation baseline. What should the service do?
options: Detect the task-distribution shift and fall back rather than adapt on a dissimilar task.
Fold the unfamiliar tasks into the support set of the closest known task family.
Run more inner-loop steps so adaptation has more chances to fit the unfamiliar family.
optionFeedback: Correct: few-shot skill is evidence about a prepared family, so shift detection plus a fallback is the designed response.
Forcing new tasks into a neighbor's support set mislabels the shift and hides it from monitoring.
More adaptation steps on a task outside the trained distribution deepen the mismatch rather than repair it.
variants.hint: What does a few-shot result actually promise about an unrelated task family?
variants.explanation: Meta-learning transfers within the meta-training distribution, so production systems detect task shift and fall back when a task is too dissimilar.
